concepts.name: Type hints are checked by tools, not enforced at runtime
`X | None` and `Literal` narrow what a value can be

questions.prompt: Given `def add(a: int, b: int) -> int: return a + b`, what happens when plain `python` runs `add("1", "2")`?

choices.text: It raises `TypeError` because the arguments aren't `int`
It converts both arguments and returns `3`
It returns `"12"`
It fails when the module is imported

questions.explanation: The Python runtime does not enforce annotations; they are for tools such as mypy, pyright and IDEs. At runtime `+` on two strings concatenates them. A type checker would report the call before the code ever runs, which is why you run one in CI.

sources.title: typing — Support for type hints — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: The Python runtime does not enforce function and variable type annotations; they are for third-party tools such as type checkers and IDEs.

questions.prompt: A module contains `def count_tokens(text): return len(text) + " tokens"`, with no annotations. What does plain `mypy` (no flags) report for it?

choices.text: An error: unsupported operand types for `+` (`int` and `str`)
Nothing: by default mypy skips the bodies of unannotated functions
A warning that `count_tokens` implicitly returns `Any` and needs annotations
An error that `count_tokens` is missing the type annotations mypy requires

questions.explanation: By default mypy skips the bodies of unannotated functions. `--check-untyped-defs` checks them, and `--disallow-untyped-defs` makes the missing annotations an error. Both are part of `--strict`, which is why a new codebase should start strict: otherwise an unannotated function hides bugs like this one.

sources.title: The mypy command line - mypy 2.3.1 documentation
sources.claim: By default mypy does not type check the bodies of functions without annotations; --check-untyped-defs checks them, --disallow-untyped-defs reports unannotated definitions, and --strict enables both.

questions.prompt: Given `def send(role: Literal["user", "assistant"], text: str) -> None: ...`, what happens with `send("system", "hi")`?

choices.text: mypy reports an error; at runtime the call still runs
Python raises `ValueError` at the call
mypy accepts it, because `"system"` is a `str`
Both mypy and Python reject it

questions.explanation: `Literal` tells the type checker the value must equal one of the listed literals, so `"system"` is a type error. Like every annotation it isn't enforced at runtime: to reject bad values from outside the program (such as model output), validate them, for example with a Pydantic model.

sources.title: typing — Support for type hints — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: Literal tells type checkers the value must equal one of the listed literals, so a different string is a type-checker error, while annotations are not enforced at runtime.

questions.prompt: `def find_user(user_id: str) -> User | None` may return `None`. What does mypy say about `print(find_user(uid).name)`, and what's the fix?

choices.text: Nothing: `| None` is only documentation, and mypy assumes the call always succeeds
An error that `None` has no attribute `name`; check `is None` first to narrow it
An error that `|` isn't allowed in annotations; use `Optional[User]` instead
An error, but only under `--strict`; the default settings allow it

questions.explanation: `User | None` means the same as `Optional[User]` (the `|` form needs Python 3.10+). mypy's optional checking is on by default, so using `.name` without handling `None` is an error. An `is None` check (or an early return) narrows the type to `User` in the code after it.

sources.claim: Optional[X] is equivalent to X | None.

sources.title: Kinds of types - mypy 2.3.1 documentation
sources.claim: Mypy disallows most operations on unguarded optional values and narrows the type after a check against None.

sources.title: The mypy command line - mypy 2.3.1 documentation
sources.claim: Strict optional checking is on by default; --no-strict-optional is the flag that turns off checking of None values.

questions.prompt: Your agent receives a tool call's arguments from the model as a JSON string. Which of these checks the values at runtime and raises an error you can send back to the model when they're wrong?

choices.text: A `TypedDict` built with `Args(**json.loads(s))`
A `@dataclass` built with `Args(**json.loads(s))`
A `Protocol` checked with `isinstance(obj, Args)`
A Pydantic model's `model_validate_json`

questions.explanation: Only Pydantic validates at runtime: it raises `ValidationError` naming each bad field, and that message makes good feedback for the model. A `TypedDict` is a plain `dict` at runtime, `@dataclass` doesn't examine its field types, and a `Protocol` describes an interface, not data.

sources.title: Models | Pydantic Docs
sources.claim: Pydantic raises a single ValidationError describing every error found, and model_validate_json() validates a JSON string or bytes payload directly.

sources.title: typing — Support for type hints — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: At runtime TypedDict instances are simply dicts, with no checking of their keys or value types.

sources.title: dataclasses — Data Classes — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: Apart from two exceptions, nothing in @dataclass examines the type given in a field's annotation.

questions.prompt: Given `class ToolSpec(TypedDict): name: str; description: str`, what is true at runtime after `spec = ToolSpec(name="search", description=42)`?

choices.text: `spec` is a plain `dict` holding `42`; only a type checker flags it
`TypeError` is raised, because the constructor checks that `42` isn't a `str`
`spec` is a `ToolSpec` instance, so `spec.name` and `spec.description` work
`description` is quietly converted to the string `"42"`

questions.explanation: At runtime a `TypedDict` instance is simply a `dict`: no validation, no conversion, and no attribute access (use `spec["name"]`). All of its checking is static: mypy checks the keys and value types wherever the dict is built or read.

sources.title: typing — Support for type hints — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: At runtime TypedDict instances are simply dicts; their key and value types are only checked by static type checkers.

questions.prompt: An agent backend has three kinds of data: a tool definition dict passed straight to the provider's SDK, an internal record of one step of the agent loop, and the arguments the model produced for a tool call. Pick `TypedDict`, `@dataclass` or a Pydantic model for each, and say why.

model_answer.summary: TypedDict for the dict handed to the SDK, a dataclass for the internal record, and a Pydantic model for the model's tool arguments, because only Pydantic validates at runtime.
key_points: TypedDict for the tool definition: it stays a plain dict the SDK accepts, and mypy checks its keys and value types statically
@dataclass for the internal step record: it generates `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` for objects your own code builds, but doesn't check field types at runtime
Pydantic model for the tool arguments: they are untrusted model output, and Pydantic validates them at runtime and raises `ValidationError`
The `ValidationError` message can be sent back to the model so it can correct the call

questions.explanation: The choice turns on where the data comes from. Data your own code builds only needs static checking, so a `TypedDict` or dataclass costs nothing at runtime. Data from outside the program, like an LLM's tool call, must be validated when it arrives, which is what Pydantic does. A Pydantic model can also generate the tool's JSON Schema with `model_json_schema()`.

questions.prompt: `class LLMClient(Protocol)` declares `def complete(self, prompt: str) -> str: ...`. `class FakeClient:` has no base class but defines the same `complete` method. Does mypy accept `run(FakeClient())`, where `def run(client: LLMClient) -> None`?

choices.text: No: `FakeClient` must list `LLMClient` as a base class to count as one
Yes: matching members with compatible types are enough for a Protocol
Only if `LLMClient` is decorated with `@runtime_checkable` so mypy sees it
Only if `FakeClient` is first registered with `LLMClient.register(FakeClient)`

questions.explanation: Protocols use structural subtyping: compatibility comes from the members a class has, not from what it inherits. mypy compares the signatures, so a `complete` with a different parameter name or return type would be rejected. `@runtime_checkable` only matters for `isinstance` at runtime.

sources.title: Protocols and structural subtyping - mypy 2.3.1 documentation
sources.claim: A class is a structural subtype of a protocol when it has all the protocol's attributes and methods with compatible types, without inheriting from it.

sources.title: typing — Support for type hints — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: A class with a matching method satisfies a Protocol for static type checking even though it does not subclass the Protocol.

questions.prompt: `LLMClient` is a Protocol decorated with `@runtime_checkable`. An object's class defines `def complete(self) -> int`, which doesn't match the Protocol's signature. What does `isinstance(obj, LLMClient)` return?

choices.text: `True`: it only checks that the members exist, not their signatures
`False`, because the runtime check compares the method's signature too
It raises `TypeError`, because the signatures don't match
`True` only if mypy has also accepted the class

questions.explanation: `@runtime_checkable` makes `isinstance` work with a Protocol, but it only checks that the required methods or attributes exist. Signatures are checked only statically, by the type checker, so don't rely on `isinstance` to prove an object really satisfies the interface.

sources.title: typing — Support for type hints — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: @runtime_checkable makes isinstance() check only the presence of the protocol's required methods or attributes, not their type signatures.

sources.title: Protocols and structural subtyping - mypy 2.3.1 documentation
sources.claim: The runtime protocol check only verifies that all protocol members exist, not that they have the correct types.

questions.prompt: Why define an `LLMClient` interface as a `Protocol` rather than an abstract base class, and how does that help you test the agent?

model_answer.summary: A Protocol is satisfied by any class with matching methods, without inheriting from it, so real clients and test fakes both fit and mypy still checks their signatures.
key_points: A Protocol is structural: any class with compatible members satisfies it, without inheriting from it
An abstract base class is nominal: a class must inherit from it or be registered
So clients you don't control, such as a vendor SDK's class, can satisfy the interface unchanged
In tests, a small fake that implements `complete` stands in for the real client, so no test calls the real API
mypy checks the fake's and the real client's method signatures against the Protocol

questions.explanation: Structural typing lets the agent depend on the shape it needs (a `complete` method) rather than on a class hierarchy. That keeps provider SDKs out of the agent's core, and a test can pass any object with the right method while the type checker still guarantees the signatures match.

sources.title: Protocols and structural subtyping - mypy 2.3.1 documentation
sources.claim: Protocols use structural subtyping: compatibility comes from having members with compatible types, not from explicit inheritance, and mypy checks those types statically.

sources.title: typing — Support for type hints — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: A Protocol defines an interface that any class with matching members satisfies for static type checking, without subclassing it.

questions.prompt: Given the generic function `def first[T](items: list[T]) -> T: return items[0]` (or `T = TypeVar("T")` before Python 3.12), what type does mypy infer for `first(["a", "b"])`?

choices.text: `Any`
`object`
`str`
`list[str]`

questions.explanation: A type variable links the return type to the argument type: `list[str]` binds `T` to `str`, so the result is `str`. That is the point of a generic function; with `list[Any]` and `-> Any`, mypy would stop checking whatever the caller does with the result.

sources.title: Generics - mypy 2.3.1 documentation
sources.claim: For a generic function like first[T](seq: Sequence[T]) -> T, the return type is derived from the argument's item type, so a sequence of str gives str.

questions.prompt: Compare `def first(items: list[Any]) -> Any` with the generic `def first[T](items: list[T]) -> T`. What does the generic version give you, and what does an upper bound on `T` add?

model_answer.summary: The generic version keeps the caller's element type in the result, so mypy can check how it's used; an upper bound limits T to subtypes of one type so the body can use that type's members.
key_points: With `T`, the return type follows the argument: `first` on a `list[str]` returns `str`
With `Any`, mypy stops checking the result, so misuse of it passes silently
An upper bound (`T = TypeVar("T", bound=X)`, or `def first[T: X]`) only accepts subtypes of `X`
Inside the function the body can then use `X`'s members, and the caller still gets back the specific type it passed in

questions.explanation: `Any` is compatible with everything in both directions, so it switches type checking off wherever it flows. A type variable keeps the specific type instead. A bound adds a constraint without losing that specificity: a function bounded by a base class can call the base class's methods and still return the caller's subclass.

sources.title: Generics - mypy 2.3.1 documentation
sources.claim: A type variable makes the return type follow the argument type, and an upper bound restricts T to subtypes of the bound, lets the body use the bound's methods, and still returns the caller's precise type.

sources.title: typing — Support for type hints — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: A type variable can be bound with TypeVar('S', bound=str) or the 3.12 syntax [S: str], meaning it can only be that type or a subtype.
